characters: Selikem Adzaho: a 14-year-old boy in a school uniform, with a notebook and a pencil behind his ear.
Mr Tsikata: the geography teacher, in a shirt with rolled sleeves, pointing at a large world map.
The world map: a classroom wall map with four countries marked by coloured pins.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious boy’s voice for Selikem; a calm, fair-minded voice for Mr Tsikata
narrationPlan.pace: Clear and measured, with a little drama at each country on the map (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light, inquisitive kora with soft percussion; a thoughtful tune at the final paragraph (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Selikem, Mr Tsikata and the school are invented. The country facts come from a 2012 analysis of formalisation approaches in Ecuador, Mongolia, Peru, Tanzania and Uganda; it is more than a decade old, so the story labels the date and tells learners not to assume the same figures today.
The story shows both what helped and what failed and says no country has fixed the problem completely. It does not name any politician, company or community.
The story does not tell Ghana what to do. It ends with a conditional argument and a reminder that lessons are not recipes.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a mining policy researcher check the summaries of the Peru, Tanzania, Ecuador and Mongolia examples against the full analysis, because only part of the document was read for this batch.
Check whether the Peruvian and Tanzanian rules have changed since 2012 and update or label the examples.
Check the argumentative paragraph against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about learning from other countries’ attempts to bring small-scale gold miners into the law. It shows successes and failures side by side and models an argumentative paragraph.
learningGoals: Describe one thing that helped and one thing that failed in another country.
Explain why a law alone does not solve a problem.
Write an argumentative paragraph with evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
beforeReading: Ask: what is the difference between borrowing an idea and copying a plan?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to sort each example into helped or fell short.
afterReading: Write an argumentative paragraph on a question such as: should a school have a compulsory tree-planting day?
Find one of the four countries on a map and note its continent.
discussion: Why might a rule that bans miners from cooperating cause problems?
What support do you think small miners need besides a licence?
reflection: When have you changed your mind after hearing both sides of a question?

support: Give an argument frame: Some people argue… However, others argue… Therefore, in my view…
stretch: Compare two of the four countries in a short report with a heading, an introduction, findings and a recommendation.

culturalNotes: Selikem, Mr Tsikata and the school are invented. The country facts come from a 2012 analysis of formalisation approaches in Ecuador, Mongolia, Peru, Tanzania and Uganda; it is more than a decade old, so the story labels the date and tells learners not to assume the same figures today.
The story shows both what helped and what failed and says no country has fixed the problem completely. It does not name any politician, company or community.
The story does not tell Ghana what to do. It ends with a conditional argument and a reminder that lessons are not recipes.
localiseThis: Ask a Ghanaian mining officer or researcher what the country has adopted or avoided from other countries’ experience.

factCheck.claim: A 2012 analysis found that Peru’s 2002 law set clear categories, lower fees and simpler environmental permits for small and artisanal miners, but the promotion policy never fully materialised, a minimum annual production applied and artisanal miners could not contract with each other; the cooperative SOTRAMI was Fairmined certified with a premium of 10 to 15 per cent.
factCheck.explanation: From a 2012 analysis of formalisation in five countries; dated.
factCheck.reference: Hinton, J. (2012), “Analysis of formalization approaches in the artisanal and small-scale gold mining sector based on experiences in Ecuador, Mongolia, Peru, Tanzania and Uganda” (delvedatabase.org).

factCheck.claim: In Tanzania, miners found licences hard to obtain and the licence term was seven years without guaranteed renewal, and a university trial gave retorts to 20 miners, 18 of whom used them for five months and recycled about 10 kilograms of mercury; in Ecuador a 1992 law legalised existing operations but credit did not develop; mercury was banned in Mongolia in 2008 but clandestine use continues.
factCheck.explanation: From the same 2012 analysis; conditions may have changed.
